title: Waakye
subtitle: Ghanaian rice and beans cooked together with a reddish colour
excerpt: The iconic Ghanaian rice and bean dish. Cooked together until the beans colour the rice a distinctive deep red. A full meal on its own with the right accompaniments.
sourceNotes: A staple Ghanaian street food and home dish, originating in the north of Ghana.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well for up to 2 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook the beans the day before if using dried.

content.text: This serves 4 and takes about 55 minutes using tinned beans. The key thing to watch is the liquid level: the rice and beans should absorb all the cooking liquid by the time the rice is cooked. Too much water leaves you with porridge; too little and the rice will be crunchy at the top.

The red colour traditionally comes from dried sorghum stalks simmered in the water. A small pinch of baking soda added to the cooking water gives a similar colour at home without any change to the flavour.
If using dried sorghum stalks, simmer them in the water for 10 minutes, then remove them. The water will be a reddish-brown colour.
Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook for 5 minutes until soft.
Add the drained beans to the pot. Pour in the 700ml water (or sorghum-coloured water). Add salt.
Bring to the boil, then add the washed rice and stir to combine.
Bring back to the boil, then reduce to a low simmer. Cover tightly and cook for 25-30 minutes until the rice is cooked and the water absorbed.
Rest 5 minutes without lifting the lid. Fluff with a fork. Serve with fried eggs, stew, fried fish, or spaghetti - the traditional waakye full plate.

items.cause: Too much water or heat too high
items.fix: Use a 2:1 ratio of water to rice and beans combined, and keep the heat very low once boiling

items.symptom: Rice is still crunchy at the top of the pot
items.cause: Not enough water or lid not sealed
items.fix: Add 50ml more water, replace the lid tightly, and cook for another 10 minutes on very low heat
A pinch of bicarbonate of soda in the water gives the traditional colour

content.text: Waakye originated in the north of Ghana and has spread to become one of the country's most popular street foods. Vendors sell it in the mornings from large pots, serving it alongside a remarkable array of accompaniments: shito (hot pepper sauce), fried fish, boiled eggs, fried plantain, and even spaghetti. The full waakye plate is one of the defining eating experiences of Ghanaian street food culture.
